source_data.original_text: g. Cliach, na Clíach, d. Clíu; ¶ al. Clíu in Maige, Clíu Máil maicc Ugaini, Clíu Muman, is in Mun., Bb. 204 b, Lbl. 646; ¶ Fir. 49, Mm. 585, Ll. 128 b, Lec. fo 204, C. 11; ¶ S. of the Shannon, Tbd. 196, Fir. 441, Lbl. 646; ¶ reached Loch Derg: Fiacha Mullethan gave Clíu as far N. as L. Deirceirc to Cairpre Finnmór maccu Muscae, "poeta regius," and also Crích Aradh fr. Cláire to L. Deircdeirc, as a reward for a poem, X. 144, Fir. 441, Bb. 71 a; ¶ in it were Ara Cliach, Arada Cliach, Aine Clíach, Cnoc Aine, Carn Feradaig, Crotta Clíach (part of the Galtees), and Temair Luachra, Ll. 128 b, ML. 76, Gc. 40, Fm. i. 46, Fen. 328, Cam. i. 426, Au. i. 96, Hb. 65, Ll. 268 b; ¶ also Áth na Déise, Bél Átha na Déise (Athneasy p. in b.Coshlea and Small County, Wes.), Fm. v. 1719, Ods. 581; ¶ Brugh na nDéise (Bruff p. and t. in b. Coshma), Fm. v. 1530, Tp., Ods, 587, this was in Déise Bec, which, as "Crích na Dési Bice," is equated with Clíu, in Ll. 263 b, 264 a, 288 a; ¶ Aney p., in S. of b. Small County is of 9,248 acres, and contains the conspicuous and most fertile hill of Knocaney and Monastir na hAine, al. Monastir an Maige; ¶ 2 m. NE. of Aney are the vill. and p. of Hospital, designated in the old records as the hospital of Aney (Pgi. ii. 304); ¶ in b. Small County; ¶ Domnach Mór Maige Aine (Tl. 307) is Donaghmore p. 21/2 m. SE. of Limk. city and in b. Clanwilliam, the only Donaghmore in c. Limk.; ¶ L. Gur tl. is in the p. Ainy; ¶ Caherhussoc p. in b. Small County in Ainy dry., Wes.; ¶ Cluain Aine p. in b. Pubblebrian (Cluain anny in 1418, Clonany in 1291), Wes.; ¶ Arada Cliach, Tl. 200; ¶ was nr and E. of City of Limk. (Of. 275), and ext. to E. of Ui Fidgente, separated fr. it by the r. Samair (Morning Star r.), Lbl. 913; ¶ Cnoc Aine Chlíach in it, Hk. 304; ¶ Knocklong, al. Cnoc Luinge, al. Long Clíach, al. Druim Damraide (Lis. 179 b) in it, and also in dry. Aney and b. Coshlea, Wes. p. 451; ¶ Cluithri Clíach i Maig Cliach, Ca. 368, Ha. 746, Hc. 2, 585 b; ¶ also Clothrén, Hc. 2, 585 b; ¶ Crotta Clíach in it, that is, the Galtee mts., which for 41/2 m. are in b. Coshlea, and 61/2 m. on its border and that of c. Cork; ¶ the Tp., p. 130, put Uaithne Cliach, Ara (Cliach), Crotta Cliach and Ui Cuanach in consecutive stanzas, and so point to their proximity to each other; ¶ Clíu Mail maic Ugaine was the l. of Curúi, son of Daire mac Dedad, al. Crích Dési Bec, Ll. 264 a, al. b. Small County; ¶ Killeady p. in Deise Bec, B. i. 1062, lviii. 647; ¶ Ane des in dry. Kilmallock, Tax.; ¶ Grian Cliach (Au. ii. 160) in it, that is the p. and dry. of Grene; ¶ Grean p., of which 5,680 acres are in b. Coonagh, and 1,511 in b. Clanwilliam; ¶ the surface hilly and the best grazing ground in Limk.; ¶ the chief seats are Derc, which commands an extensive view of the brilliant circumjacent country, and Sunville, Pgi. ii. 288; ¶ Sunville reflects Grian; ¶ Pallasgreen vill. is in this p.; ¶ Greene dry. comprised p. Cahercorney (in b. Small County), Tax.; ¶ Liscormick, al. Aglishcormic p., of which is in b. Coonagh, and in b. Clanwilliam, Tax. and Pgi.; ¶ Kilkellane, or Kilcullane p. (31/2 m. SE. of Sixmile-bridge), in b. Small County, also Dronmon Church of the Manor of Any in dry. of Aherlow, Wes.; ¶ also Corbally, Tax., and Kilfrush p. S. of Hospital in b. Small County, Wes.; ¶ also Aglishcormick p. in b. Clanwilliam, Grean p. in b. Coonagh, Ballinlough p. in b. Coonagh, also Tuath Aoise Gréine or Tuogh p. (in b. Owneybeg, 4 m. NE. of Pallasgreen), Wes.; ¶ Aes Gréine, q.v., included Castleconnell and Singland; ¶ again, Uaithne Cliach, q.v., was in Clíu, which is the b. of Owneybeg, Tp. 128, Au. i. 432, and dry. Owney; ¶ in the dry. Owney are Caherconlish, Oola, Caherelly nr L. Gur, Rathjordan, Wes.; ¶ it seems also that Clíu, al. Aine, included Glynn in b. Shanid, as the knights of Glynn are called the Knights of the Valley of Anye, Sw. an. 1215; ¶ Dún Cuille of Clíu was in Uib Cuanach, Lec. 208 (Doon in b. Coonagh); ¶ as it seems from Ll. 268 b that Temair Luachra was in Clíu Máil maic Ugainí, and Luachair ext. into cc. Cork and Limk., and was conterminous with Claonghlais, a district in b. Upr. Connelloe, c. Limk. (Tp. lxxiii., lxxv.), so did Clíu. From all this I gather that Clíu included E. half of c. Limk., plus the b. of Owney and Ara to Killaloe (at L. Derg)—viz., the bb. Owneybeg, Coonagh, Clanwilliam, Small County, Coshma, Coshlea, Pubblebrien, Upr. Connelloe (and even Shanid?); ¶ if the extent of Clíu is, perh., overstated by me, it is unduly restricted by others:—as co-ext. with bb. of Coonagh and Small County (MacCarthy in Ui.), in b. Coshlea (O'Curry, Mm. 480), in b. Coshlea, betw. Knockany and Slievereagh (O'Don., Fm. v. 1648), in SE. of c. Limk. (Hennessy, Au. i. 96); ¶ the following refer (?) to Clíu Muman: Cath Cliach, Hk. 326, Of. 206, Lbl. 325 a, K. 132 a, 158 b, Au. i. 44 (Regio, terra, campus) Cliach, B. xlii. 27, Cs. 225, 235, 237, Ll. 146, 156 b, Lec. 217, Ll. 339 a, Sto. 18 a; ¶ v. next three words.

Bec. in Meath; ¶ D. Ethra in Iarthur Mide and D. Tire da-locha in Connacht are of the Clann Ebir, Ll. 328; ¶ Delmnai, as., the people of Delvin, Au. i. 412; ¶ Delmne, now b. Garrycastle, King's c., Au. i. 200; ¶ Na Seacht nDealbhna .i. D. Mór a Mighi, D. Beg a Mighi, D. Eathra a n-Iarthar Mighi, D. Tíri dá loch, D. Sidha Neanta, D. Feadha En, 7 a Connachta atait na Ceithri Dealbhna fadheiridh, I. 89 a 2; ¶ the seven Dealbhna in Conn's Half were possessed of lands got by the race of Eibher, such as the Coghlans. The seven Dealbhna are D. mhór, D. bheag, D. Eathra, D. iarthair-Mhídhe, D. Shithe neannta, D. Chúile-fhobhair, and D. Thíre dha Loch, K. 145 b; ¶ desc. fr. Sumann, son of Lughaidh Dealbhaeth, 3rd son of Cas. Their possessions in Connacht comprised the b. of Moycullen, c. Galw., anciently called Dealbhna Feadha and D. Tire da Loch, betw. L. Oirbsean and L. Lurgan (L. Corrib and Galw. Bay); ¶ D. Cúile Fabhair; ¶ al. Muintir Fathaidh, comprising 14 townlands E. of L. Corrib, "O Fathartaigh's country; ¶ " Dealbhna Nuadhat, nearly all included in b. Athlone, betw. the Suck and the Shannon, Lct. 104; ¶ na Coíg Delbna, named fr. Delb-aeth, Ca. 358; ¶ fr. context some of them were in Meath when Carn Fiachach meic Néill was; ¶ leg. na secht nDelbna.

The sub-territories of Airgialla were: Ui Nialláin (bb. of Oneilland, c. Arm.); ¶ Ui Bresail (now in bb. Oneilland); ¶ Ui Echach (bb. of Iveagh, c. Down); ¶ Ui Meith [Macha] (pp. of Tullycorbet, Kilmore and Tehallan c. Mon.); ¶ Ui Tortain (around Ardbraccan, c. Meath); ¶ Ui Briuin Archaill (in b. Dungannon, c. Tyrone); ¶ Trí Tuatha (here comprising Fir Lemna, Ui Cremthainne and Síl Dubthir of Lct.); ¶ Dartraige al. Dartraige Coininnsi (b. Dartry, c. Mon.); ¶ Fera Manach (Fermanagh), Fernmag (b. Farney, c. Mon.); ¶ Mugdorn and Ross (Cremorne with p. Carrickmacross, and p. Clonany, c. Mon., and adjoining parts of Louth and Meath undefined), Fen. 367, 371, and Lct. 144 to 154, which adds Leithrinn; ¶ cf. Mr. 28; ¶ the 2 Kings of Airgialla -viz., Daimin, King of A. from Clochar Deasa to Finncharn Sléibe Fuaid, and Aed King of A. from Finncharn Sléibe Fuaid to the Boyne, K. 160 b; ¶ in Argialla, were—Cnoc Báne (in b. Clogher), Ll. 24 a, Fm. i. 102; ¶ Achad Raithin i. bFeraib Cell, Md. 354; ¶ Loch Dabaill, Fm. i. 40; ¶ Machaire Arnaidhe in A. in d. Ard Macha i cCondae Muinechain, Md. 78; ¶ Mag dá ghabhar Fm. i. 46, Datraige, Au. iii. 474; ¶ Mag Fernmaige, Fm. i. 36; ¶ Mag Macha, Fm. i. 10; ¶ part of Monaghan, Of. 365; ¶ Tech Tálain, Fg. 104, Md. 138; ¶ Ath Firdead or Ardee in Louth (the Cenel nEogain went to Ath Firdead in aid of the Airgialla—so A. extended to Ardee, Au. ii. 132). Fearann Airgiall, luaiter lind, ó Áth in imairg co Find, ó Glind Rige siar co se, co Bearramain a mBreifne Gor Chosain Muirceartach mear, re claind na Colla cneis-gel, ó Glinn Con, ruathar na creach, co h-Ualraig Daire dairbrech. The land of A. let it be mentioned by us, From Ath an Imaig to the Finn, From Glenn Righe westwards directly, to Bearramain in Breifne. Until the vigorous Muircheartach wrung From the descendants of the fair skinned Collas, From Glen Con in a battle of plunders, To Ualraig at the oak-bearing Derry—Mr. 142; ¶ Airgialla = d. of Clogher, Fep. Fg. 5, Con. 38 a; ¶ Conb. 25 a; ¶ Au ii. 538, 262, 308, Lc. i. 186, 200; ¶ Airgialla, np, Ll. 26 a. Au. ii. 26, Sil. 50, Ch. 316, K. 149 b, Ll. 26 a; ¶ ap. Airgiallu, Ll. 24 a, Lb. 29; ¶ they were of the Cenél n-Eogain, Ca. 150; ¶ descendants of the three Collas, K. 149 b, Ar. 162; ¶ Airgiall, gp. Ll. 303 b, Fia. 69, Ca. 352, Beo. 13 a, Bb. 51 a, Mr. 28, Cg. 44, F. 72, Au. iii. 106; ¶ np. Origiallaigh, Au. iii. 258, Airgéill, Stokes Tl. Index; ¶ the np. is Oirgialla in Tl.; ¶ Oirghiallaigh is wrong; ¶ dp. dinaib Airgiallaib, Au. i. 322; ¶ Eochaidh Doimhlen, from whom are the Airghialla in Erin, in Alba, and wherever they are, Lec. 176, Fir. 303; ¶ the Airgialla and úi Néill descend from Fiacha Sroptine, son of Coirpre Liphechair, Ll. 332; ¶ the Oirgialla possessed what includes the present Counties of Louth, Armagh, Monaghan, Londonderry, and Tyrone; ¶ but were deprived of Tyrone and Derry by Niall circ 400, Tp.; ¶ Oriel, uriel in Louth, Armagh and Monaghan, Of. 361, Mr. 30, Fia. 34; ¶ Cluain Eoais a bFeraibh Manach, nó gomadh etir Feraibh Manach acus Oirghialla atá, Md. 94; ¶ Mainistir Bráthar Minúr do thinsgnadh a Muinechan re linn Feidhlim Meg Mathgamna do bheth i n-a righ ar Oirghiallaibh (A.D. 1462), Au. iii. 206; ¶ Oirghialla seems here to have extended to and included the town of Monaghan; ¶ "the principal families of the A. were the MacMahons, O'Carrolls, O'Hanlons, Maguires, O'Hanraghtys, MacKennas, &c.; ¶ , &c.; ¶ their country comprised the counties of Louth, Armagh, and Monaghan, and the greater part of Fermanagh," O'D. Mr. 8; ¶ MacCaba, Constabla Oirghiall, Au. iii. 28; ¶ Mag Mathgamna airdrí Oirgiall, Au. iii. 50; ¶ Oirghiall, or Oirghiall-Mic-Mathghamhna, MacMahon's country, or Oriel, Ci. airi ... source_data.original_text: ns. Cualu, Pd. viii. 38; ¶ gs. or gp. Cualann, Cualand as Clanda Cualann, Codex St. Pauli, Tph. ii. 295, Lu. 84 b, Cs. 322, Au. i. 330, Lis. 36 b, Lct. 4, 12, 14; ¶ ds. Cualainn, Proc. R.I.A. vii. 186, Gc. 8, Fm. ii. 640, S. p. 346. As to its extent there are various views: O Don. says "Crích C. was included in the present c. of Wick." (Fm. i. 26); ¶ again, coext. with "the half b. of Rathdown in N. Wick. and adjoining the c. of Dubl. Harris places this territory several miles out of its proper locality, for he describes it as a territory in the E. and maritime part of c. Wick., comprehending the N. of b. Arklow and S. of b. Newcastle" (Lct. 13). "Coext. with b. Ballinacor N. and b. Rathdown, c. Wick., and S. half of b. Rathdown, c. Dubl." (MacCarthy, Au. iv. 103). "A district of c. Wick." (Of. 195). Crích C., l. of O Kelly, in Wick. (Obr.). The following places are in it: Aband Dea, Bd. 8, Ll. 159; ¶ Inber nDea, Bd. 8, Lis. f. 4a; ¶ Tochar Inbir Móir (Arklow) in Crioch Ua nEnechglais Chualann, Lg. 77, Hx. 881, Bb. 23 a, Fm. i. 27; ¶ Ostium Dee (Coolenorum), A. 2 b 2, i.e. Arklow; ¶ Cell na Manach, where St. Coemgen studied (Kilnamanagh tl. in p. Tallaght, b. Uppercross, c. Dubl.) Cs. 916; ¶ Bruden Dá Derga, It. i. 96; ¶ Dún Delginnsi, Fm. i. 26, Hk. 302; ¶ Bray r. and Oldcourt, Prim. 846; ¶ Brea and his Cland died in Crich C., Pd. 58; ¶ Tiprait Casra (? Tipperstown nr Stillorgan or Kiltipper nr Tallaght), Lu. 98 a; ¶ Tech gConaill (Stagonil p., al. Powerscourt, 3 m. SW. of Bray), Md. 138; ¶ Tech mic Dimmai in Uib Cellaig Chualand, F. 167; ¶ Rath Oinn (Rathdown, O'D.), Fm. i. 26; ¶ Heremon had 2 kingly raths, one named Rathonie in the l. of Kwalann and Rathbehic over the r. of Feoire, Ac. 28; ¶ Áth Cliath (Dublin), Rc. xvi. 284; ¶ Aonach Seara in Críoch na Moirrighna, S. of Coirthe Chualann, Lis. 196b; ¶ Coirthe Cualann, S. of Inber Life (? the Steyn, at site of Crampton monument nr T.C.D.), Lis. 196 b; ¶ Óe Cualann (= Ear of Cualann), al. Aei. C. nr Dubl., Pd. 56, seems to be the same as Druim Ing (it may be the ridge on towards Kilmainham), Pd. 60; ¶ betw. Sencharaid or Senchoraid and Cuilend (Glencullen ?), Pd. 62, trí háird Erenn, Cruachan Aigle, Aei C., Benn Boirche, I. 190 a; ¶ Glenn Cualann; ¶ Tír C.; ¶ Clár C., Tp.; ¶ Bóthar C., Ll. 278 a, 318 a, Fir. 840; ¶ Slige C., Mm. 259, 453. C. included also the following tribes:—Críoch na Moirrighna, S. of Coirthe C., Lis. 196 b; ¶ Crioch hua nEnechglais, incl. Síl Forannain hui Minloscuin, Ll. 15, and Tóchar Inbir Moir, Lg. 77, Hx. 881, Bb. 23 a, Fm. i. 27; ¶ Ui Bruin C., F. 46, i.e. Fir Cualand, Bdd. 37, incl. Ui Manadain, Lec. 205, and Caenraige or Caenraide, Ll. 389; ¶ Ui Ceallaig C., in c. Wick., desc. fr. Maine Mail, Of. 310; ¶ Fir C., Lct. 4, 5, 12, acc. to Inquis. of 21 Apr. 1636 "containeth in length fr. Barnecullen by E. and S. and Glassyn ... kie to Pollcallon by W. the Windgates (present name)—viz., 5 m. in length and 4 in breadth ... all desolate only Powerscourt, Killcollin, Beanaghebegg, Benaghmor, the Onenaghe, Ballycortie, Templeregan, Kiltagarrane, Cokiston, Ancrewyn, Killmolinkey, Ballynbrown, Killeger and the Mainistir; ¶ " Onagh, Annacrivey, Kilmalin, Killegar are tls. in p. Powerscourt, c. Wick. From all this C. seems to ext. fr. *Arklow to the Liffey, and to be coext. with d. of Glendaloch; ¶ other refs. are: Ct. 53, 63; ¶ vastatio Lagen .i. tír C. usque Glenn duorum stagnorum, Au. i. 310, Fm. i. 428; ¶ they went fr. Waterf. to Glenn dá locha and to Fera C., Igb. § 22; ¶ Cremthand of Bend Etair is called Cr. Cualand, as if C. incl. Howth, Pd. 52; ¶ C. seems to be in Leth Cuinn, Fm. ii. 640; ¶ cuirm C. was a prerogative of the K. of Lein., Lct. 4, 14. Under Bóthar Cualann, supra p. 120, Ingean na hAlaboidigh (Miss Hollywood) is wrongly translated Miss Talbot. [* Cualu included even the b. of Arklow, in which were Ui Einechlais Cualann, O'D., Fm. i. 528 v. U Einechlais].

source_data.original_text: there Óenach Carman was held; ¶ was on site of t. of Wexf. (O'Curry, Mm. ii. 38, O'Don. in Lct. and Fm., and Hen. Lc. i. 34); ¶ was in S. of c. Kild. (Hen. Au. i. 345); ¶ "was really n the present c. Carlow" (Hen. Au. i. 567); ¶ was in c. Kild. (Dr. M`Carthy in Index to Annals of Ulster); ¶ Hen., in language too long to quote, twice expresses his disedification at "such an acute topographer" as O D.'s equation of Carman with (Loch) Garman, "for which there is no authority"; ¶ he objects—1, that if Fedlimid, marching from Cashel to meet the K. in c. Kild., went round by Wexf., he would probably get very short shrift from the Ui Ceinnselaigh; ¶ 2, that when Mac Gillapátric inaugurated his succession to the kingship of Ossory by celebrating the Aenach Carman "he was not likely to go for that purpose to Wexf., where he would probably get a very warm reception from the Ui Ceinnselaigh"; ¶ in support of Henn.'s objections I will add two stronger ones: 3, in Fm. ii. an. 1079, it is said that O Conor Faly's land was plundered by the men of Teffia and Cairbre (who, however, were defeated), and next O Conor Faly celebrated the Oenach Carman; ¶ fr. this O'D. infers that O C. Faly claimed the highest authority in Lein., as that fair was held at Wexf.; ¶ it is incredible that O C. F. made good his claim to predominance over Lein. by celebrating an Oenach at Wexf. while the Danes were there in force and the K. of Lein. and of the Foreigners and of Leth Mogha was still powerful; ¶ his country was 60 m. fr. Wexf., as the crow flies, and his family had little power in the 11th century, when he held the Oenach, and are only thus noticed by the Four Masters: the Lord of Ui Failge killed by his own people in 1051; ¶ the L. of Ui F. blinded by his brother Conchobur in 1070; ¶ the L. of Ui F. slain in battle by Conchobur O Conchobuir in 1071; ¶ in 1079 this Conor O C. Failey defeats the men of Cairbre and Teffia, and afterwards celebrates the Oenach Carman; ¶ in 1089 Donnchad, Lord of Lein. (or of Ui Ceinnselaigh), was slain by Conor O C. Failghe by an unfair advantage (the Annals of Ulster and the An. of Loch Cé say "a suis occisus est"); ¶ in 1094, this Conor, Lord of Ui Failghe, was taken prisoner by O Brien, K. of Mun., and in 1115 O Brien and the Foreigners of Dub. defeat the Leinstermen in a battle in which were slain the Lord of Ui Ceinnselaigh and Conor O C., Lord of Ui Failge, and his sons; ¶ in 1092 Donnchad, son of O C. Faley, was killed by his own brothers; ¶ a man with such a record as Conor O C. Faley did not obtain supremacy in all Lein. and celebrate it at Wexf. after a triumphant march of 70 or 80 miles; ¶ and I conclude that his Oenach Carman was in Ui Failge or nr. it. Though I believe that the Oenach Carman of Mac Gillapatric and O Conor, of not a metaphorical expression, was near their borders, where I will identify a Carman, I do not wish to deprive the Faithche of Wexf., now called the Fáith, or Fair-green, of the glories of the ancient Oenach Carman fully described in the Books of Lein. and Ballymote. Yet all the evidence seems to show that Carman was a large plain on the banks of the Burren and the Barrow, which unite at the town of Carlow; ¶ here the Kings of Lein., whose palace of Dind Ríg was close by, held every three years an Óinach—that is, a Grand Council, of their Sub-Kings and Chiefs—an exhibition, a cattle-show, a fair and races; ¶ these Kings and their civil and military advisers showed great judgment and tact in selecting for the Óinach a place at the geographical, social, political, and military centre of Lein., nr. the royal palace, which was the rendezvous of the warriors of Lein. when about to march against their foes, as we learn fr. Cath Ruis na Ríg, and nr. or not far fr., the five great tribal divisions of the Province now represented, respectively, by the dioceses of Ossory, Leighlin, Kildare, Ferns, Glendaloch (and Dublin); ¶ from this central place also they could quickly send a "punitive" expedition if Mun. or Meath were mean enough to invade their borders during the Óinach; ¶ that shows it ought to have been there; ¶ but, then, Irish eccentricity might have held the Oinach Carman at Loch Carman, at the town of Wexf., where O'Donovan and O'Curry place it; ¶ I answer that that Carman was nr. the r. Burren in Idrone (Bairenn Cliach), which joins the Barrow at Carlow; ¶ nr. Idrone (Clíu, gen. Cliach); ¶ nr. Dind Ríg, which is nr. Burren and Idrone; ¶ nr. Berna Cleighi; ¶ nr. Mag Lifi; ¶ nr. Mag Mesca and Ui Failge; ¶ in close connections with laces nr. or not far fr. r. Burren; ¶ by its Óinach, in close and sole connection with clans whose lands meet nr. the Burren. 1. Carman was nr. r. Burren: -Bairend Charman i Caillich Carman at Bairend Cliach and at Berna Cleithi, Lec. 461; ¶ Bairend Carmen co Cailliu Carmuin ic Bairind Cliach ic Bernae na Cleithe, I. 150 b; ¶ Caille Carman at Bairend Chliach ic Bairind Carman ic Berna na Cleithi, Lbl. 428; ¶ Digais, wife of Carman, and mother of Bairend fr. whom is named Bend Bairne Carman (Bairne is gen. of Bairend), Lec. 461; ¶ Bairend Charman at the r. Bablua (Dindsenchus Bairne Cermain, Ll. 194); ¶ Bablua, q. v., is Bairend; ¶ at Coilliu Cermain and at Babluan al. Bairend Clíach at Bernae na Cleite, Bb. 195 b; ¶ Bairend Cearmain .. i Colbu Cearmain 7 ic Babluan al. Bairenn Cliath ic Bearnaidh na Cliath, Sa. 20 b 1; ¶ 2. Carman was in or nr. Idrone; ¶ see Clíach in No. 1, the gen. of Clíu in Uib Dróna, A. 18 b, Ll. 23 a, 129 a, Fm. i. 88, Hk. 406, Ch. 43; ¶ 3. nr. Dind Ríg on the Barrow; ¶ ar bruach Bearbha idir Cheithiorlach 7 Leithghlenn, K. 118 b, betw. Carlow and Lethglenn, Of. 172; ¶ Dind Ríg in Mag n-Ailbe, Tig. Rawl., B. 502, fo. 1 b; ¶ 4. nr. Berna Cleithe, v. No. 1; ¶ 5. nr. Mag Lifi: Carman Liphi. Ll. 169 b; ¶ Mag Lifi included Maistiu, or Mullaghmast (A. 10 a) within 10 m. of Carman, indeed Mullaghmast has been identified with Carman, as we shall see infra; ¶ 6. nr. Mag Mesca and Ui Failge: Mag Mesca at Aenach Carman, Lbl. 418; ¶ Aenach Carmuin, al. Aenach Sengarmain in Mag Measca, Bb. 193 b; ¶ Sencharman in Mag Measca i n-Uib Failge, I. 149 a 2 (Ui Failge included Mag Fea and Cell Osnadh in c. Carlow, nr. r. Burren, Bc. 15); ¶ 7. in close connection with places nr. or not far fr. r. Burren: Rí Railend (5 m. S. of Athy), Rí Carman, Rí Fothart Osnadaigh (b. of Forth, c. Carlow), the Ui Dróna (b. Idrone, c. Carlow), Ui Bairrchi (b. of Slieve Margy, in Queen's Co.), Ui Buide (b. of Ballyadams, Queen's Co.), are grouped together in Lct. 210—214; ¶ Aillend árd Carmon clothach, and Almu (Will of Cathair Mór), Lct. 202; ¶ liach liomsa Cnoc Almaine 7 Aillenn, liach lom Carman 7 fér dar a rótta .. all n-árd n-Almaine, flaith nár Náis, Fm. ii. 572; ¶ mór liach Life gan Cerball (K. of Lein.), liach lemsa Cnoc Almaine 7 Allenn, liach lem Carman, Fia. 220; ¶ Braein Carmain ... ór-al Alman, Fm. ii. 652; ¶ Triacha long do laechraid Liamna .. dligid im na crícha im Charmon tricha banmog, tricha bó, Lct. 40 (Liamain was in Mag Laigen, al. Mag Lifi, F. 83); ¶ Flann Temra don Tailltenmaig, Cerball don Carmain Cinaig, Fm. 570, Ch. 182 (i.e., as Tailltiu was to Temair so was Carman to Dind Ríg?); ¶ Slogad la Feidlimid (ríg Caisil) corici Carmain; ¶ slogad la Niall (rí nErenn) ar a chenn corice Mag n-Ochtair, Au. i. 344, Fm. i. 460; ¶ Cath Maige Ochtair isin tealaig ós Cluain Conaire a ndes, Fm. i. 212—that is, the K. of Cashel reached S. of Kild., and marched to Cloncurry, in N. Kild., where he was awaited and defeated by the K. of Ireland; ¶ 8. Óinach Carman in ancient and in comparatively modern times was always and only held by kings, sub-kings, and chiefs, whose lands met nr. the junction of the Burren with the Barrow. This is clear from the description of it in Ll. and Bb. given in Mc. ii. 40, as well as from the Irish Annals:—On the right of the K. of Carman, al. K. of the Barrow or Dind Ríg, sat the K. of Ossory, on his left, the K. of Ui Failgi; ¶ in accordance with the will of Cathair Mór, the Uí Failgi (al. Síl Rosa Failgi), the Laigsi, the Fotharta (or Laigsi Fothairt), and the Clann Condla, al. Ossairgi, were the chief leaders of the celebrations; ¶ the Uí Dróna, in whose land it was, displayed unbounded "hospitality" (oegidacht hUa nDróna); ¶ and the K. of the Barrow distributed the prizes, Mc. iii. 526–547; ¶ in historical times one K. of Ossory and his Ossorians held the Óinach Carman an. 1033, and one K. of Ui Failgi did the same in 1079, Fm. ii. 826, 914, Au. i. 566, Lc. i. 34; ¶ Carman was one of the 7 chief cemeteries of Erin, at it were many meeting-mounds, 21 raths, 7 mounds, 7 plains or fields (without a house) reserved for the Óinach; ¶ it may be said that cúan (harbour), ráth-lind (bounteous water), and bruachaib (banks), applied to Carman, would not suit the t. of Carlow; ¶ I think so: the tide goes higher than St. Mullins, and from New Ross to Athy (10 miles N. of Carlow) the Barrow is navigable by barges; ¶ a writer in Pgi. ii. 399, i. 316, got very nr. the real Carman; ¶ "the Rath or moat of Carman or Mullaghmast nr. Ballytore, 6 miles E. of Athy, its site is a gently sloping hill crowned by an extensive rath, and nr. it are 16 mounds, on which the elders of the States of S. Lein. sat in council, these mounds are held in veneration by the peasantry." Gen. Carman (Fm. ii. 1142, i. 48, Sb. 4 a, Fm. ii. 826, Lct. 14, 210, Lc. i. 34, Mc. iii. 526), and dat. Carmain (Fm. an. 903 and bis in Mc. iii. 536) point to nom. Carmu or Carma; ¶ but nom. Carman, Cormon, Cormun (Sas. 1274, Ll. 215 a, 169 b, Lct. 202, Mc. iii. 526, Pd. viii. 38, Fm. an. 903); ¶ gen. Carmain, Fm. i. 44, Au. i. 566; ¶ Carmuin, Sr. 64 a bis; ¶ dat. Carmon, Cormun, Ll. 127, 296 b, Bb. 46 b; ¶ Carman, Fm. i. 76, 460, ii. 570, 652.

Navan and Slane, where are a round tower and ch. ruin; ¶ the only Donaghmore in Meath nr c. Mon., and yet 15 m. S. of it; ¶ this puts the bb. of Slane in M. Breg; ¶ there is Donaghmore tl. in Louth 4 m. E. of b. Farney, but as it is in b. of Upr. Dundalk, and only 2½ m. SW. of Dundalk t., it seems not in Bregia; ¶ the NW. Louth parts of pp. of Iniskeen and Killanny are of Donaghmoyne dry., c. Mon., and in N. of M. Breg; ¶ Dunleer (Lann Léire), Mellifont (Mainister Mór Drochit Atha, Lis. 201 a), Monasterboice (Mainister Boite), Clonmore (Cluain Mór Fer n-Ardai i mBregaib, Lis. 9 b), in b. Ferrard, 2½ m. This possible barrow was discovered under c. 2.1m of peat during the construction of a bog road in 1881. It was recorded by Wood-Martin (1887-8) as a circular platform (diam. c. 9m) with a cairn of large, narrow stones centrally positioned. Enclosing the platform was a shallow fosse, a low earthen bank and an outer fosse. There were four piles of stones located at regular intervals upon the bank. The structure appears to have been destroyed during the road construction. Its exact location was not recorded. 

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 19 January 2011

In 1887, during the construction of a bog road, traces of a number of fires were identified between c. 1.5m and c. 2.1m below the peat. All of the hearths were paved with stones. One large example was semicircular in plan (diam. c. 9m) (Wood-Martin 1887-8, 278-81). Some of these features probably represented the remains of fulachtai fia. They appear to have been partly or entirely destroyed during the road construction. Their exact location was not recorded.

Listed in the SMR (1989) as ‘cist –possible’, this record refers to a slab-lined structure which was uncovered in 1950 on the edge of a stream at a depth of c. 3 feet [0.9m] below the surface during county council drain-cleaning works in Ballyeeseen Td., near Dromore West (NMI Correspondence Files). It was thought to be a grave and was examined by a member of An Garda Síochána who sent a report to NMI. It was describes as being 'about 6ft square' [c. 1.8m], with two opposing sides each constructed of a single large slab (H c. 0.45m), and the other two sides constructed of smaller slabs, with ‘two stone posts about 6 inches [0.15m] square one on either end.’ The floor was paved with stone slabs. It was filled with clay and small stones but no bones were found. Given the absence of bones, and its location beside a stream, the possibility exists that the structure was not a cist grave but the stone-lined trough of a fulacht fia. The exact location of the find was not recorded.

This record refers to field boundary which was noted in this area in the early 1990’s. It was listed in the RMP (1995) as ‘field wall’, with a centre point at IG 139050 331420 (approximately ITM 539014 831426): the source of this record is unknown and there is no field report from the 1990’s on file. The constraint area as defined in the RMP (1995) encompasses a broad, relatively level expanse of blanket bog straddling the junction of three townland, Camcuill, Owenbeg and Bellafarney. A stream flows N through the W half of the area. The N third of the area is under coniferous plantation. The southern two thirds of the area are covered in low heather, sedge and bog grasses, broken by occasional sphagnum pools and old bog cuttings. An inspection on 30th May 2014 found no trace of the field wall within the area of open bog. The density of trees and ground litter made an effective inspection impossible within the area under forestry. The exact location of the field wall remains unknown.

Not marked on any edition of the OS 6-inch map. Situated on the E side of a penninsula which juts NNE-wards into Ballisodare Bay. A dense layer of oyster shells (T 0.3m - 0.4m) in a matrix of dark soil is visible along most of a 400m long length of coastline. At the NE of the penninsula the lens is overlain by a layer of sand and is underlain by a stony subsoil. The greatest concentration is at a D-shaped projection of land at the SE of the penninsula. Firstly there is a lens at the shoreline. Secondly there is a naturally-occurring pool of water c.45m back from the shoreline. Between the shore and the pool are large quantities of midden material. The greatest concentration (dims. c.50m N-S; c.30m E-W) is adjacent to the E shoreline of the pool. (Synge 1985, 128)

On a gravel knoll, upon which three other prehistoric monuments: a mound barrow (SL040-155001-), a pit burial (SL040-155002-) and a short cist (SL040-155003-) have been identified. This monument was uncovered during sand extraction in 1972 and excavated by Ryan in the same year. Small, subrectangular short cist (dims. 0.54m NW-SE; 0.33m NE-SW; D 0.44m) whose sides are defined principally by five slabs set on edge augmented by smaller packing stones. The N, E and S sides are each formed by a single slab while the W side is delimited by of two thinner slabs placed parallel to each other. The landowner had displaced one of the end stones. He told the excavator that this end of the cist had been closed by two stones set on edge with one resting upon the other. These stones were not identified. The capstone was curvilinear (dim. 0.56m; T 0.19m). It only proved possible to guage one side of the pit (dim. 0.74m; D 0.45m) which had been dug to house the cist. The upper 0.35m beneath the capstone was filled with gravel. However upon the floor of the cist was a deposit containing cremated bone and flecks of charcoal. The cremated bone is thought to indicate the presence of two individuals: an adult male and second adult of indeterminate sex (1972:178). No artifacts were uncovered (Cahill and Sikora 2011, Vol. 1, 429-435).

NMI Correspondence Files (1954) record the discovery of human bones during quarrying activities on the land of a Mr. James Lavelle in Ballinteane townland. The quarry was described as being 'at the back of the dwelling house of the owner of the land...and about 100 yards from it.' The bones were uncovered following the removal of clay from an area of bedrock, at a depth of c. 0.60m below the surface. The bones were severely damaged but upper and lower jaw bones, complete with teeth, confirmed that they were human. No evidence of a grave was noted. The site was inspected by the Gardai who sent a report to the National Museum. A few days later an object described as 'what appears to be the head of a stone axe' was found close to the site of the bones, and a small bell, possibly of brass, was also recovered. A feature which was described as a fire-place made of stone bricks was also found (Cahill and Sikora 2011, Vol. 2, 511-512). According to local information, the farm, which has since changed ownership, is location in the N of the Ballinteane townland, c. 500m W of the cross roads at Kilglass Parish church. The exact location of the quarry pit, however, is unknown.

Located in the intertidal zone on the NE shoreline of Coney Island at the SW end of Sligo Harbour.
This monument was discovered in August 2014 on the N shore of Coney Island. The uppermost sections of a rectangular, stone, cist-like structure were exposed in the sand below the high-water mark. Excavation (14E0478) of the structure revealed that it consists of a trough-like feature defined by six limestone slabs set on edge (internal dims. 1.49m E-W by 0.69m N-S and c. 0.5m deep) and floored internally by two flat slabs. The trough is orientated E-W. Both the E and W ends are closed by a single slab. The N and S sides were defined by two stones, a long slab and a short upright narrow stone beside it. The uppermost 0.22m of each of the main sidestones was visibly discoloured indicating the level of exposure to the elements and seawater. The lower section of the fill of the trough contained a large quantity of heat-shattered and fire-cracked stones, and some charcoal. The absence of evidence of burning on the slabs and within the structure precludes the possibility that it might have been a hearth. No artefacts were recovered. The excavation revealed that the pit for the structure originally had been cut into the natural beach sand and, although initially interpreted as a possible cist, the evidence suggests that the remains are more than likely to be a stone-lined trough of a fulacht fia. The trough was backfilled after the excavation and remains in situ. It has been dated to the late Bronze Age (908-810 cal. BC; pers. comm. J. Bonsall). The monument is known locally as a 'lover's wishing well' or a 'sailor’s grave’. 

When the trough was first recorded in 2014, no evidence of an associated mound of burnt stone was visible. On 17th July 2015 a roughly circular spread (diam. c. 8m) of pinkish-brown, angular heat-shattered stones was noted 2m to S of the trough. It was exposed by the eroding action of a high tide which scoured away the covering sand layers (pers. comm. Dr. J. Bonsall, Masc Project, Sligo IT). Immediately to SE of the stone spread, a midden (SL008-204----) of oyster shell and periwinkle shells was also exposed. When inspected on 21st July 2015, tidal action had again largely concealed these features with a covering layer of sand.

On the E shore of Lough Gara, in a secluded bay near the outflow of Lough Gara into the Boyle River. The bay has silted up and the crannog is now on dry land, in a stony meadow beside a substantial drainage ditch. The vegetation consists of bushes and meadow grass. The low-cairn crannog (11.3m N-S; 16.2m E-W; H 0.97m above the meadow), the centre of which consists of an oval plateau (5m N-S; 6.6m E-W), is overgrown with low grass and some small shrubs. The surface is even and only occasional stones protrude. The plateau is surrounded by an edge that slopes sharply to the N, W and E, while to SE there seems to be a berm (Wth c. 2-2.4m) tapering to W. The edges have a number of boulders and stones protruding, possibly forming a line of stones to the N. There is a small collection of stones outside the plateau at E. A lacustrine enclosure (SL045-016----) and another crannog (SL045-008----) are c. 250m to NW and WSW, respectively. (Fredengren 2002, BOYL 079)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

Located on the sandflats/seabed in Dumcliffe Bay, 7m N of the S shoreline of the bay.

A natural spring, which bubbles up through the sandy floor of the seabed, is enclosed by a rough wall (diam. 2m; H 0.3-0.4m) of low contiguous stones, with a gap (Wth 0.7m) at NW. The wall is one stone wide and one to two stones high. The stones are seaweed-covered. The well is visible and accessible only at low tide. According to local tradition, it is dedicated to St. Columcille, and curative properties are attributed to the waters (pers. comm. Tamlyn McHugh, 2014). The Pattern Day is on the 9th of June. There is a low-tide routeway (SL008-182----) across the bay c. 40m E of the well.

Casey (1999, 195) recorded a possible promontory fort in Ballygilgash townland at OS 6-inch co-ordinates 168 202 and NGR G437351 (equating approximately with ITM 543647 835111), and described it follows: ‘An oblong headland lies along the coast beside a stream near Donagh Pier. The area is one of fertile grazing and steep cliffs lie on either side of the site. A small headland, measuring 14m east-west by 4m north-south is cut off from the mainland by a 1m deep, 3.5m wide fosse with traces of a low earthen bank on either side. A path runs along the cliff edge into the interior which is featureless. It is unclear whether or not this fosse is man-made.’ The area was inspected in December 2014. The Ballygilcash coastline consists of a storm beach bisected at its E end by the mouth of a river. There is no pier in the vicinity. There are cliffs extending N from the W end of the beach but no headland projects from them. No evidence of a promontory fort was found at the location of the recorded co-ordinates, or along the storm beach, or at a narrow projecting spit of land at the mouth of the river. The landscape on the Ballygilcash coastline does not match Casey’s description; it is possible that the locational detail is incorrect. The exact location of the possible promontory fort remains unknown.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Located in the intertidal zone on the NE shoreline of Coney Island at the SW end of Sligo Harbour.
This midden, which was exposed by the eroding action of a high tide, was first noted and recorded on 17th July 2015. It consists of a densely concentrated, irregular spread (L 20m NW–SE; Wth 1-5m; T 0.003-0.01m) of oyster and periwinkle shells. Within the general mixed spread of shells, there are discrete pockets which consist only of periwinkles or only of oyster shells. Small quantities of charcoal were noted, and some periwinkle shells have a blackened, burnt appearance. A single piece of chert was found. Immediately adjacent at NW, there is a concentration (diam. c. 8m) of angular heat-shattered stones associated with a fulacht fia (SL008-205----), the stone-lined trough of which is located 5m to NW of the midden. Bordering the SW edge of the midden, a compact, hard dark-coloured sandy layer (10m x 5m) appears to represent old beach deposits, which the midden directly overlies. (pers. comm. Dr. J. Bonsall, Masc Project, Sligo IT). When inspected again on 21st July the midden was once more largely concealed by sand washed in by the tide.

Wakeman (1893, 82–4, fig. 40) recorded this fragment of a cross-slab in the 1880s in Teach Molaise (SL001-001005-), but its current whereabouts are unknown.

Slab fragment (H: 0.195 m, W: 0.15 m) incised with the upper two thirds of an outline cross and an inscription in the upper left quadrant. The inscription simply reads: CRUX (Translation ‘Cross’)
At the crossing the false relief strands are separated thin incised lines, but they soon diverge so that the arms expand steadily from the crossing to terminate in large bulbous terminals. The terminals are decorated with hollow false relief circles, and that in the upper arm features a tiny central boss.
 
This fragment and another cross-slab fragment (SL001-001048-) may be part of the same cross-slab.

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

The source of this record is contained in account by Seaton F. Milligan of a number of ringforts in the county (1879). Having described the cashel (SL015-059001-) he states: ‘A little above the cashel high up in the precipitous limestone cliff there is a cave, almost concealed from view, which has unmistakable indications of having been a dwelling-place of primitive man. It is situated in an almost impregnable position that a few could defend against a multitude, and as such was a natural stronghold of a type in use ages before the days of artificial forts. The principal cave is 55 feet long, 5 feet wide, and 9 to 10 feet high; about its centre a second cave branches off to the right for a distance of 25 feet. Outside the entrance is the midden where the ancient occupiers pitched their refuse, and also, apparently, cooked their food. We dug here through a layer of charcoal, and also found a quantity of bones of various animals, and turned up a small bronze buckle as well.’ (ibid., 579-80). It has not proved possible to locate this cave (SL015-102001-) or midden (SL015-102002-).

This record refers to one of three cairns noted by Wood-Martin (1882, 114). He recorded them as 'three grass-covered cairns' which were located 'on the opposite side of the road' to a souterrain (SL016-061001-). He refered to them again in a later account as 'three mounds resembling grass-covered carns' which were 'not far distant' from the souterrain (Wood-Martin 1887-8, 297). The other two cairns are SL016-060001- and SL016-060003-. The exact location of this cairn is unknown.

Locating in forestry-covered blanket bog, on the broad, flat top of a ridge flanked at W by the Easkey River valley and at E by the small valley of the Fiddaungarrode stream. This record was not listed in the SMR (1989). It refers to a ‘field wall’ which was first noted in the early 1990’s and was listed in the RMP (1995) at IG 139960 327300 (equating to ITM 539924 827307). A post row (SL017-089002-) was also recorded here. The source of this record is unknown and there is no field report from the 1990’s on file. The area was inspected in 2014 but no trace of the field boundary was found. It is likely that the monument was incorrectly located at the time of the original inspection. It may have been damaged or destroyed during forestry works. Its exact location remains unknown.

On the N side of a holy well (SL038-120002-) which cuts into the SE perimeter of a stepped barrow (SL038-120001-) and on the W side of a stream. A roughly rectangular block of sandstone (L 1m; Wth 0.4m; H 0.44m), perforated obliquely through its thickness. The perforation (diam. 0.13m) is cylindrical, smooth and regular but constricts slightly at the centre of the stone. The stone represents the lower stone of what would have been a pair of millstones from a horizontal-wheeled mill. According to local information, this millstone was found in the stream c. 30m to SE of its present location where it is marked and named 'Bullaun' on the OS 6-inch map: it was placed at the holy well in recent times. The exact location of the mill is not known.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

Recorded by Wakeman (1893, 80) ‘in a modern recess in the Cashel wall [SL001-001001-].’ The current whereabouts of the stone are unknown.
Slab (220 by 160 mm) with upper left hand corner and base broken off. The surface was filled with most of the upper and left arms, a complete right arm and short section of the shaft of an incised cross with triangular terminals. There was a circular expansion at the crossing decorated with a false relief boss. Parts of a horizontal inscription remain in two lines positioned above and below the horizontal cross members.
CRUX
RETE
Translation: ‘Cross of Rete’

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

Date of upload: 12 March 2018

This cross-slab was recorded by Wakeman (1893, 91) as lying on the ‘Saint’s Bed’ (SL001-001006-) within Teach Molaise (SL001-001005-). The current whereabouts of the stone are unknown.
Thin slab (H: 0.43 m, W: 0.28 m [after Wakeman]) with inscription. Wakeman says that the inscription was ‘in the Irish character’ and that the letters were ‘extremely small and closely packed, and slanting in a running-hand style.’ He was only able to decipher a few of the letters, ones which he thought ‘were probably capitals.’ His attempts at deciphering by rubbing failed and he did not illustrate the slab.

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

Date of upload: 20 February 2018

This cross-slab was recorded by Wakeman (1893, 99, fig. 47) in the Men’s Cemetery (SL001-001029-) within the ecclesiastical enclosure/cashel (SL001-001001-), but its whereabouts are now unknown.
Cross slab fragment (0.45 m by 0.45 m). Wakeman’s drawing (fig. 47) depicts a cross with a short, simple shaft, but arms and head with expanded terminals from which diverging spirals are developed. All members carry a simple two-strand interlace pattern, with triquetera-like terminations and a simple knot at the intersection. Two much smaller, plain crosses are incised to the right of the principal cross (Wakeman suggests that there were two others in a symmetrical or opposed position left of the main cross on a missing fragment of the stone).
The design closely resembles that of a cross-slab (SL001-001077-) – now in the Schoolhouse/OPW conservation store – and it is possible that these are one and the same slab.

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

Date of upload: 20 February 2018

This cross-slab was recorded by Wakeman (1893, 101, fig. 48) in the Men’s Cemetery (SL001-001029-) within the ecclesiastical enclosure/cashel (SL001-001001-), but its whereabouts are now unknown.
Cross slab fragment (0.25 m by 0.38 m). The central cross on this oblong slab is represented by Wakeman with expanded terminals to the arms and feet, with divergent spirals or at least hooks developed from the foot, and a spear-shaped or diamond-shaped expansion of the head, containing a small circle. Set about this main cross, in the quadrants, are four simple crosslets with expanded terminals.

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

Date of upload: 20 February 2018

This cross-slab was recorded by Wakeman (1893, 118, fig. 59) near the entrance to the ecclesiastical enclosure/cashel (SL001-001001-), but its whereabouts are now unknown.
Slab fragment (H: 0.685 m, W: 0.535 m) whose face was originally filled with a ringed, slightly shafted, outline cross. The upper arms (0.274 m) are only marginally shorter than the shaft (0.305 m), and unlike it they are decorated with semi-circular terminals with straight butts. The ring comprises four curving false relief bands which abut the arms 0.18 m from the crossing. Within this ring the cross arms curve inwards to form hollow arm pits.

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

Date of upload: 20 February 2018

Formerly set into an altar-like structure at Tobernalt holy well (SL014-238----) it consisted of a rectangular slab bearing the coat-of-arms of the French family below which were the initials EF. This stone had been moved from the Dominican priory at Sligo (SL ) to Tobernalt prior to 1893. A corresponding matching counterpart survives at Sligo Abbey where it is set against the wall under the tower. The stones undoubtedly formed part of a larger memorial to Andrew FitzJohn O’Crean and his wife, Ellen French. The present location of this stone is unknown. (Timoney 2013)

A large piece of window tracery was found in the graveyard (SL020-109002-) of St Fechin's church (SL020-109001-) on the site of an early monastery (SL020-109005 -). This probably originated from the Augustinian abbey in Abbeytown (SL020-108----), c. 250m to the W. (M. B. Timoney 2002, 157-8, n. 14). During a graveyard clean up in 1995 and 1996, a number of architectural pieces, a Romanesque font and a medieval graveslab (SL020-109010-) were found (M. B. Timoney 2002, 149-59). One of the architectural pieces included a piece of window tracery (SL020-109016-) that was probably from the Augustinian abbey (SL020-108----), c. 250m to the W in Abbeytown (ibid. 157-8, n. 14).

At a leacht (SL001-011----), known as ‘Laghta Patrick’, at the east end of the Inishmurray.
O’Donovan (1836 'Sligo Letters' OS Letters, no. 36. Royal Irish Academy) commented that Laghta Patrick (SL001-011----) was 'a square pile of stones, on the top of which an ornamental stone cross stands'. No further details are known about this slab. The cross was not observed by any authorities since O'Donovan and may have been long since washed away or broken up on the nearby storm rubble of Rue point. 
Limited archaeological investigation (licence: 99E0382) in 1999 identified the base of the leacht (SL001-011----), but no trace of the cross was found on or around the excavation site or on the storm-rubble beach below (O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin  2008, 239-241).

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.
